title: Promise Pool
statement:
Write `promisePool(functions, n)`, an `async` function that runs the asynchronous functions in the array `functions` with **at most `n` of them in progress** at any moment. Each `functions[i]` takes no arguments and returns a promise: calling it starts its work, and it stays in progress until that promise resolves.

Start the functions in index order. Right away, start as many as the limit `n` allows; then, each time a running promise resolves, immediately start the next function that has not been started yet, if there is one. The promise returned by `promisePool` resolves as soon as every function's promise has resolved (at once when `functions` is empty); the value it resolves with does not matter. No promise ever rejects.

Each case describes `functions` as a list of delays: `functions[i]` returns a promise that resolves `functions[i]` ms after it is called. The answer is `[times, total]`, where `times[i]` is the moment (in ms from the start) at which the promise of `functions[i]` resolved, or `null` if it never did, and `total` is the moment the promise of `promisePool` resolved.
constraints: Each functions[i] resolves after an integer delay from 0 to 1000 ms
notes:
## Intuition

Think of the pool as `n` **workers**. Each worker repeatedly takes the next function that nobody has started, calls it, and waits for its promise before taking another. With `n` workers there are never more than `n` promises in progress, and a slot is refilled the moment its promise resolves, because that worker's `await` resumes right then. The pool is finished when every worker has run out of functions, which `Promise.all` on the workers detects. (The brute force keeps a set of running promises instead and, when the set is full, waits with `Promise.race` for any one of them before starting the next.)

## Approach

1. Keep `nextIndex`, the index of the next function to start, shared by all workers.
2. A `worker` loops while `nextIndex < functions.length`: it claims `index = nextIndex`, advances `nextIndex`, calls `functions[index]()` and awaits its promise.
3. Start `poolSize = min(n, functions.length)` workers and collect their promises in `workers`.
4. `await Promise.all(workers)`: it resolves when the last worker finishes, that is, when the last function's promise has resolved.

Claiming and advancing happen before the `await`, with no pause in between, so two workers can never take the same index.

## Example 1, step by step

Delays `[300, 400, 200]`, `n = 2`.

- At 0 ms two workers start: the first calls `functions[0]` (300 ms) and the second `functions[1]` (400 ms); `nextIndex` is now 2.
- At 300 ms `functions[0]` resolves. The first worker wakes up, claims index 2, and `functions[2]` (200 ms) starts.
- At 400 ms `functions[1]` resolves; the second worker finds no function left and finishes.
- At 500 ms `functions[2]` resolves, the first worker finishes, and `Promise.all` resolves. The answer is `[[300, 400, 500], 500]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k) work for k functions plus O(n) to start the workers; the waiting lasts as long as the schedule itself.
- Space: O(min(n, k)) for the workers.

## Pitfalls

- Starting in batches (run `n`, wait for **all** of them, run the next `n`) leaves slots empty. In Example 1 that gives `[[300, 400, 600], 600]`.
- Calling every function first and only then limiting the waiting does not limit anything: a call is what starts the work.
- Forgetting the empty case: with no functions, the pool must still resolve, at time 0.
- With threads, a pool is a semaphore with `n` permits; in JavaScript one thread runs everything, so a shared counter is safe as long as it is read and advanced without an `await` in between.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `nextIndex` | index of the next function no worker has started |
| `worker` | loop that keeps one pool slot busy |
| `index` | the function a worker has just claimed |
| `workers` | the promises of the running workers |
| `poolSize` | how many workers to start: `min(n, functions.length)` |

narration.1: promisePool is async, so it hands the caller a promise that resolves when the body finishes.
narration.2: nextIndex is shared by all workers: the next function that nobody has started.
narration.3: A worker keeps one slot of the pool busy.
narration.4: While some function has not been started, this worker takes the next one.
narration.5: Claim the index before awaiting, so no other worker can take the same function.
narration.6: Advance the shared index for the other workers.
narration.7: Calling the function starts it; the worker waits here until its promise resolves, then loops to refill its slot.
narration.11: No more than n workers, and no more workers than there are functions.
narration.12: Start the workers one after another, all at time 0.
narration.13: Calling worker() runs it until its first await and returns its promise.
narration.15: The pool is done when every worker has run out of functions, so wait for all of them.
